Random Generation from the Modified Half-Normal Distribution

Source: R/rmhn.R
rmhn.Rd

Draws random variates from the Modified Half-Normal (MHN) distribution with parameters alpha, beta, and gamma.

Usage

rmhn(n, alpha = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 0, method = c("auto", "rtdr", "sun"))

Arguments

n

Number of variates to draw: a non-negative number no larger than .Machine$integer.max, truncated to an integer, so that n = 0 returns numeric(0). Following the base R convention of rnorm() and rgamma(), if length(n) is not 1 the number required is taken to be length(n), so that a zero-length n also returns numeric(0); NULL is an error.

alpha

Shape parameter (\(\alpha > 0\)). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

beta

Rate-type parameter (\(\beta > 0\)), the coefficient of the Gaussian tail \(\exp(-\beta x^2)\); larger values pull mass toward zero. Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

gamma

Tilt parameter (\(\gamma \in R\)), the coefficient of the exponential tilt \(\exp(\gamma x)\). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 0.

method

Sampling algorithm. One of "auto" (default), "rtdr", or "sun". See Details.

Value

A numeric vector of length n. As in rnorm, an element whose parameters (after recycling to length n) are NA or NaN, or lie outside the parameter space (alpha or beta not positive and finite, or gamma not finite), is NaN, with a single warning "NAs produced", and draws no random numbers. A zero-length alpha, beta or gamma makes every element NA, with the same warning. The parameters must be numeric (double, integer or logical): a factor, a character string, a complex number, a list or NULL is an error. If a rejection sampler accepts none of 1000 proposals for an element (for a subnormal shape, none of 1000 draws of the proxy below, each of up to 1000 proposals), that element is NaN, and a single warning reports how many draws were affected; the acceptance rates of the samplers make this vanishingly unlikely. Where the distribution lies beyond the largest double precision number, and at some other extreme values, rmhn instead stops with an error for the whole call (see Details).

Details

The MHN density is $$f(x \mid \alpha, \beta, \gamma) = \frac{2 \beta^{\alpha/2} x^{\alpha-1} \exp(-\beta x^2 + \gamma x)}{\Psi[\alpha/2, \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}]} \quad (x > 0)$$ where \(\Psi[a, z] = \sum_{n \ge 0} \Gamma(a + n/2) z^n / n!\) is the Fox-Wright function \({}_1\Psi_1[(a, 1/2); (1, 0); z]\). rmhn does not evaluate \(\Psi\); the rejection-sampling kernels cancel it out. The one exception is the weight of the origin, \(1 / (1 + w)\), that it draws for a subnormal shape (see Subnormal shapes below).

The default parameters alpha = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 0 correspond to the half-normal distribution \(\mathrm{HN}(1/\sqrt{2})\).

Choice of sampler

The method argument selects the rejection sampler:

  • "auto" (default): Uses closed-form special cases when applicable (\(\gamma \approx 0\) -> sqrt-Gamma, \(\alpha \approx 1\) -> truncated normal, where \(\approx\) means within sqrt(.Machine$double.eps), for the tilt on \(|\gamma|/\sqrt{\beta}\); away from \(\gamma = 0\) and \(\alpha = 1\) themselves the law drawn is then within a total variation distance of \(8.6 \times 10^{-9}\) of the one requested). Otherwise it selects the faster of the provably correct samplers, as measured by timing them against each other on an Apple M1 Ultra, for the parameter region and the number of variates drawn per setup. The choice changes only the speed, not the law drawn, and the crossings move from machine to machine. For \(\gamma > 0\) it uses RTDR (Gao & Wang 2025) when \(\alpha < 1\). When \(\alpha > 1\) it uses RTDR if \(\alpha \le 2^{59}\), the tilt \(z = \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) is at most \(2\sqrt{\alpha}\) and enough variates share a setup, and Sun et al. (2023) Algorithm 1 otherwise. Enough means 5, 25, 50 or 100 variates for \(z \le \sqrt{\alpha}\), and 25, 50, 100 or 1000 above it, for \(\alpha < 10\), \(10 \le \alpha < 1000\), \(1000 \le \alpha < 10^8\) and \(\alpha \ge 10^8\) respectively, and 5 or 25 where RTDR's setup starts next to the mode (see below). For \(\gamma < 0\) it uses RTDR above \(\alpha = 2^{59}\) (see below). Up to that shape it uses Sun et al. Algorithm 3 when fewer than 25 (\(\alpha < 0.1\)), 5 (\(0.1 \le \alpha < 1\)), 10 (\(1000 \le \alpha < 10^5\)), 25 (\(10^5 \le \alpha < 10^8\)) or 50 (\(\alpha \ge 10^8\)) variates share a setup, for \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta} > 10^{150}\) and where RTDR cannot place the distribution (see below), and RTDR otherwise, which for \(1 < \alpha < 1000\), and wherever RTDR's setup starts next to the mode, means at any number of variates per setup. For \(\alpha > 1\) that setup searches for the two contact points of RTDR's envelope. It starts the search next to the mode \(m\) of \(\sqrt{\beta}X\) at very large shapes, where it builds the envelope relative to the mode (from about \(2.4 \times 10^{12}\) to \(3.1 \times 10^{12}\) at moderate tilts, from about \(2.3 \times 10^{13}\) near a tilt of \(-\alpha/e\), and from about \(4.5 \times 10^{13}\) at any tilt), and under a very strong negative tilt, \(z < -10^{10}\sqrt{\alpha}\); the default method decides this with the setup's own test. Elsewhere the search walks the two points in from \(m/2\) and \(m + \max(1, m/2)\), and from a shape of about 1000 on that makes RTDR's setup dearer than Algorithm 3's. The number of variates per setup is counted as n for scalar parameters, and as n divided by the least common multiple of the lengths of alpha, beta and gamma, the period after which the recycled triples repeat, rounded down, where a setup is kept for each position within that period (see below). Otherwise it is 1: parameters given as vectors of length n count one per setup, as in a Gibbs sampler, even when equal triples are grouped into runs, and such a call draws what the loop of single draws would. A long run of one triple is drawn fastest by its own scalar call.

  • "rtdr": Use the Relaxed Transformed Density Rejection method of Gao & Wang (2025) for the general case. Gao & Wang bound the acceptance probability below by \(1/e \approx 0.368\) uniformly over the parameter space where the contact points of the envelope lie in their band (their Eq. (7)); the search for them does not always reach that band, and the acceptance measured stays above the bound there too. The closed-form special cases are still taken first: a negligible tilt draws from the square root of a Gamma, and \(\alpha \approx 1\) from a truncated normal. Both are exact samplers of their special-case law, which next to \(\gamma = 0\) or \(\alpha = 1\) is within a total variation distance of \(8.6 \times 10^{-9}\) of the law requested, and faster than any rejection scheme, so no sampler choice overrides them, except that a negligible tilt above \(\alpha = 2^{60}\) is drawn by RTDR (see below). Where RTDR cannot place a law of tiny shape under a strong negative tilt, Sun et al. Algorithm 3 is used instead (see below). Note: Gao & Wang (2025) use the parameterization \((\lambda, \alpha, \beta)\) with density proportional to \(x^{\lambda - 1} \exp(-\alpha x^2 - \beta x)\); the mapping to the Sun et al. parameterization used here is \(\lambda \leftrightarrow \alpha\), \(\alpha \leftrightarrow \beta\), \(\beta \leftrightarrow -\gamma\) (sign flip on the linear term).

  • "sun": Use the Sun et al. (2023) algorithms for the general case, with the same closed-form special cases taken first. Algorithm 1 is used when \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\alpha > 1\); Algorithm 3 is used when \(\gamma \le 0\), up to \(\alpha = 2^{59}\), beyond which the call stops with an error (see below). The combination \(\alpha < 1\) with \(\gamma > 0\) is unsupported and triggers an error, unless a special case answers it first.

Vector parameters and setups

Vector parameters are recycled to length n following standard R rules: only the first n elements of each parameter are used, and any further elements are silently ignored, matching the convention of rnorm.

Internally the setup of the chosen sampler is built once for each run of equal consecutive \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) triples and, when short parameter vectors whose triples repeat after a period of at most 256 draws are recycled over at least four such periods, at most once for each position within that period, so passing parameters grouped by triple, or as short recycled vectors, is faster than calling rmhn inside an R loop. Grouping saves setups but does not change the number of variates per setup counted above, and so not the choice of sampler.

Reproducibility

Under one seed, method = "rtdr" and method = "sun" draw one stream whatever n: the first k draws of rmhn(n, ...) are those of rmhn(k, ...), and draws split over several calls are those of one call. The default method does not keep this, as it chooses its sampler from the number of variates per setup (see above): rmhn(4, 5, 1, 2) and the first four draws of rmhn(100, 5, 1, 2) come from different samplers. Its stream therefore changes with n, with how the parameters are arranged, and with a version of the package that moves a threshold, although the law drawn does not. Where the draws must not depend on n, as when a pilot run is compared with the main one, set method = "rtdr" or method = "sun".

Limits of double precision

Double precision limits which laws can be sampled, and how finely. Every sampler draws from the exact law and rounds the draw to double precision, and a draw below the smallest positive double is returned as 0. As \(\alpha\) or \(\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) grows, the distribution narrows around its mode relative to the mode itself, and a rounding error that moved every draw alike, such as that of a computed mode, would become a visible part of its standard deviation. Wherever such a shift could exceed a few times \(10^{-7}\) of a standard deviation, the draws are placed from the mode computed to about twice double precision, so that each is the exact draw rounded once. R's rgamma, which the square-root-Gamma closed form and Sun et al. Algorithm 3 draw from, rounds \(\sqrt{a - 1/2}\) and the scale, and so shifts every variate of shape \(a\) alike by up to about \(3 \times 2^{-53}\sqrt{a}\) standard deviations, \(2.5 \times 10^{-7}\) at \(a = 2^{59}\). Algorithm 3's own setup, which rounds the shape, power and rate of its Gamma proposal, adds a shift of the same kind, and its draws were measured to shift by up to about \(4.5 \times 2^{-53}\sqrt{\alpha}\) standard deviations in all (\(3.8 \times 10^{-7}\) at \(\alpha = 2^{59}\)). Both are used only up to a Gamma shape of \(2^{59}\) (about \(5.8 \times 10^{17}\)), at \(\alpha\) up to \(2^{60}\) and \(2^{59}\) respectively. Above \(\alpha = 2^{60}\) a negligible tilt of either sign is drawn by the Normal proposal of Algorithm 1 centred at the mode (by RTDR under method = "rtdr"): Sun et al. (2023) state Algorithm 1 for \(\gamma > 0\) and Theorem 1 for \(\gamma \ge 0\), but centred at the mode the Normal envelope holds for either sign. Above \(\alpha = 2^{59}\) a negative tilt that is not negligible is drawn by RTDR under the default method, while method = "sun" stops with an error.

The RTDR sampler stops with an error for the whole call once the standard deviation is no larger than the spacing of the double precision numbers at the mode: from \(\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) of about \(9 \times 10^{15}\) (\(2^{53}\) at \(\beta = 1\)), and, for \(\gamma \le 0\), from \(\alpha\) between \(2^{103}\) and \(2^{106}\) (\(1.0 \times 10^{31}\) to \(8.1 \times 10^{31}\)). The standard deviation of the law over its mode \(m\) is about \(1/\sqrt{2\alpha}\) at \(\gamma = 0\) and \(1/\sqrt{\alpha}\) under a strong negative tilt, where the law is close to the Gamma distribution with shape \(\alpha\) and rate \(-\gamma\), and the doubles at \(m\) are between \(2^{-53} m\) and \(2^{-52} m\) apart; so the stop comes between \(2^{103}\) and \(2^{105}\) (\(4.1 \times 10^{31}\)) at \(\gamma = 0\) and between \(2^{104}\) and \(2^{106}\) under a strong negative tilt, depending on where \(m\) falls between two powers of two. There the law is normal to far below double precision, with mean \(m\) = mhn_mode(alpha, beta, gamma) and variance \(1/((\alpha - 1)/m^2 + 2\beta)\), and can be drawn from directly. Sun et al. Algorithm 1, which the default method uses for such laws with \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\alpha > 1\) (up to \(\alpha = 2^{59}\) their tilt exceeds \(2\sqrt{\alpha}\), and above that shape Algorithm 1 serves at any tilt), and the truncated normal of \(\alpha \approx 1\) do not stop there: their draws are placed at the mode to within a few units in the last place, so that they take only a few distinct values near it. For a strongly negative tilt the law approaches the Gamma distribution with shape \(\alpha\) and rate \(-\gamma\), which Algorithm 3 draws at any tilt up to its shape limit. RTDR works with \(\sqrt{\beta}\,x\), or for \(\alpha \le 1\) with its logarithm \(y = \log(\sqrt{\beta}\,x)\), and cannot place the law in three cases. The first is where \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) passes the largest double. The second is for \(\alpha \le 1\) and a finite \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\): the mode of \(\log(\sqrt{\beta}X)\) is the logarithm of about \(\alpha\sqrt{\beta}/|\gamma|\), and where \(\alpha\) is below about \(2.5 \times 10^{-324}\) (half the smallest positive double) times \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\), which needs \(\alpha\) below \(4.4 \times 10^{-16}\), that number rounds to 0; almost all the mass of \(X\) then lies below the smallest positive double. The third is for a shape of a few, where \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) comes within a small factor of the largest double. In the second case, and in the first for \(\alpha < 10^{-15}\), but for a subnormal shape (see below), method = "rtdr" draws from Algorithm 3, which samples the law exactly there; otherwise it stops and names that Gamma law. The default method uses Algorithm 3 in all three cases, except where \(-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) passes the largest double at a shape above \(2^{59}\); there it stops as RTDR does. Where the distribution lies beyond the largest double precision number, no draw can represent it, and every sampler, the closed forms included, stops with an error.

Subnormal shapes

A subnormal shape, below the smallest normal double \(2.2 \times 10^{-308}\), is drawn as the mixture its law is (see the Details of dmhn): 0 with probability \(1 / (1 + w)\), the probability of a value below the smallest positive double, and otherwise from the peak, as the law of the shape \(2^{-60}\) above \(\sqrt{\beta} x = 1\), which has the peak's density there to within a relative \(4 \times 10^{-18}\), by the sampler method selects for that shape. The choice between 0 and the peak compares one uniform variate with \(1 / (1 + w)\), and so has the resolution of the generator, \(2^{-32}\) for R's default. Where \(1 / (1 + w)\) is 1 in double precision, below a tilt of about 52 (53 at the smallest shapes), every draw is 0 and uses no random number; a shape from \(2^{-1022}\) up is drawn by the samplers above, which use random numbers there too, so that the stream after the draws moves as the shape crosses \(2^{-1022}\) although every draw is 0 on either side. A refusal names the shape asked for.

References

Sun, J., Kong, M., & Pal, S. (2023). The Modified-Half-Normal distribution: Properties and an efficient sampling scheme. Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods, 52(5), 1591–1613. doi:10.1080/03610926.2021.1934700

Gao, F., & Wang, H.-B. (2025). Generating modified-half-normal random variates by a relaxed transformed density rejection method. Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation, 1–25. Advance online publication. doi:10.1080/03610918.2025.2524551

Robert, C. P. (1995). Simulation of truncated normal variables. Statistics and Computing, 5(2), 121–125. doi:10.1007/BF00143942

See also

dmhn, mhn_mean, mhn_var

Examples

set.seed(1)
rmhn(10, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 0.5)
#>  [1] 0.4882149 1.7209460 0.2702322 0.5039321 1.0199839 0.8549756 0.5065696
#>  [8] 1.1410072 0.7866116 1.0854880

# Vector parameters are recycled to length n.
set.seed(1)
rmhn(5, alpha = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
#> [1] 0.4429697 0.7989284 0.5821857 1.4320656 2.2998471
